results.message: My brother took his own life last year. What would your church have said about him?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We grieve with you. One of our bishops spoke to this, and he began with pity. He wrote of Christian virgins taken captive, some of whom were violated. He who kills himself is a homicide. The more innocent a man is of the offence he dooms himself for, the guiltier of his own death he is. His words do not say what became of any person who died this way. They say nothing about burial.

We kept the dead in mind at the Lord's altar. Possidius says Augustine had psalms of penance copied and wept over them as he lay dying: “And he did this himself in the last illness of which he died. He ordered the very few penitential Psalms of David to be copied for him. As he lay in bed during his sickness, he would look at these sheets hanging on the wall and read them. And he wept freely and constantly. He did not want his attention broken by anyone. So about ten days before he left the body, he asked those of us who were there to let no one come in to him. The only exceptions were the hours when the doctors came to examine him, or when food was brought to him. This was kept and done, and he had all that time free for prayer. Up to the very moment of his last illness he preached the Word of God in the church. He preached without ceasing, with vigour and power, with a clear mind and sound judgment.”

The man who taught that even good Christians must repent before death did it himself. We cannot tell you what an ordinary believer felt standing at the altar on an ordinary week. We can tell you we kept the baptized dead in mind there, and that your brother belongs at that table if he was one of us.

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV, independently re-located this session; Doc_01 SS2); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII; Doc_01 SS2); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo (lpc.story.the-psalms-on-the-wall)

sentences.sentence: Possidius says Augustine had psalms of penance copied and wept over them as he lay dying: “And he did this himself in the last illness of which he died. He ordered the very few penitential Psalms of David to be copied for him. As he lay in bed during his sickness, he would look at these sheets hanging on the wall and read them. And he wept freely and constantly. He did not want his attention broken by anyone. So about ten days before he left the body, he asked those of us who were there to let no one come in to him. The only exceptions were the hours when the doctors came to examine him, or when food was brought to him. This was kept and done, and he had all that time free for prayer. Up to the very moment of his last illness he preached the Word of God in the church. He preached without ceasing, with vigour and power, with a clear mind and sound judgment.”
